content.text:
All confirmed — the `changeAlarm()` method (with `set.remove(alarm); set.add(alarm)`) and `disableExpiredAlarms()`/`init()` (iterating `for (Alarm alarm : set)` while calling `enable()`, which triggers `changeAlarm()`) persisted unbroken from f1939c88 all the way to 62dd6a1, where the bug was finally fixed.

## Bug-Introducing Commits
BIC: f1939c88e3f8602b993b1b2e30bda8b4adb34409

## Reasoning

**(1) Investigation:** I traced the history of `Alarms.java` (formerly `AlarmsManager.java`) backward from the fix commit `62dd6a1`. That fix removes `set.remove(alarm); set.add(alarm);` from the `changeAlarm()`-style write path, and replaces a loop that called `enable(alarm.getId(), false)` on every expired alarm inside `for (Alarm alarm : set)` with a version that mutates the alarm object directly (`alarm.setEnabled(false); writeToDb(alarm.getId());`) without touching the `set` collection. This is the classic fix for a `ConcurrentModificationException`: don't remove/re-add elements of a collection while iterating over it with a for-each loop.

Walking further back, I found the same `for (Alarm alarm : set) { ... enable(...) ... }` pattern already existed one commit earlier (`717ab02`, moved from a `disableExpiredAlarms()` method into `init()`), and further back still in `disableExpiredAlarms()` since it was first written. I then located the commit that introduced both halves of the bug simultaneously: `f1939c88` (2012-07-22).

**(2) The introducing change:** In `f1939c88`, the class was refactored from being purely DB-backed (querying a `Cursor` each time) to caching alarms in an in-memory `Set<Alarm> set` field. This commit:
- Introduced `private int changeAlarm(Alarm alarm)`, which does `set.remove(alarm); set.add(alarm);` after writing to the DB.
- Introduced `disableExpiredAlarms()`, which iterates `for (Alarm alarm : set) { ... enable(alarm.getId(), false); ... }`, where `enable()` calls `set(alarm)`/`changeAlarm(alarm)` internally.

Because `enable()` (called from inside the for-each loop) transitively mutates the very `set` being iterated, any time an expired-and-eligible alarm is found, a `ConcurrentModificationException` is thrown at runtime — most notably at app boot in `init()`, since `disableExpiredAlarms()`/its equivalent is invoked there.

**(3) Evidence:** 
- `git show f1939c88 -- .../AlarmsManager.java` shows the field `set = new HashSet<Alarm>();` being added, along with `changeAlarm()`'s `set.remove(alarm); set.add(alarm);` and `disableExpiredAlarms()`'s `for (Alarm alarm : set) { ... enable(...) ...}` — all added in the same commit.
- I checked every intervening commit (`c502083`, `391f995`, `98749d1`, `255bcf6`, `e86f6cf`, `dd67bef`, `506f53e`, `e9bf160`, `6f5a4ed`, `717ab02`) between `f1939c88` and the fix `62dd6a1`; none of them touch the `set.remove/set.add` lines or restructure the loop to avoid the aliasing — the unsafe pattern is present continuously until `62dd6a1` removes it.
- The fix commit's diff directly targets this exact pattern (renaming `changeAlarm` usages to a `writeToDb` that no longer touches `set`, and inlining the expiry-disable logic to avoid calling back into a `set`-mutating method during iteration), which is strong confirmation that the bug being fixed is this concurrent-modification issue rooted in `f1939c88`.

I'm confident in this attribution — the mutation pattern (`set.remove`/`set.add` inside a method invoked from a for-each over `set`) is unambiguous, and it's traceable to a single commit that introduced both the collection and the unsafe call path together.
